items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to prohibiting smoking in
certain outdoor areas
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S2655

SPONSOR: STAVISKY
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to prohibiting smok-
ing in certain outdoor areas

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This bill would restrict smoking in certain outdoor areas.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1. The public health law is amended by adding a new section
1399-o prohibiting smoking on any municipal or state operated park, or
pedestrian plaza.

Municipal or state operated parks include boardwalks, marinas, play-
grounds, recreation centers and all other property, equipment, buildings
and facilities under charge or control of any state or local government.
Pedestrian plazas are any area designated by the department of transpor-
tation for use as a plaza, which may contain benches, tables or other
facilities for pedestrian use.

Section 1 of this bill also labels areas where the provision shall not
apply. These areas are sidewalks immediately adjoining parks, parking
lots, theatrical productions, and any route through any park strip,
median or mall that is adjacent to vehicular traffic.

This section also exempts the Adirondack Park and Catskill Park as
defined by section 9-0101 of the environmental conservation law from any
provisions of this bill.

Section 2. Section 1399-v of the public health law, as added by chapter
244 of the laws of 1989 is amended. It assigns a civil penalty of fifty
dollars for each violation.

Section 3 of this bill sets the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Worldwide, smokers toss an estimated 4.5 trillion butts every year.
Cigarette butts have been the leading item found during the Interna-
tional Coastal Cleanup Project. (Conducted by the Center for Marine
Conservation) Cigarette butts are not biodegradable. While the paper and
tobacco of cigarette butts are biodegradable, their cellulose acetate
filters are not. Cellulose acetate, a form of plastic, can persist in
the environment for many years.

Localities throughout the country are now acting to ban smoking on
public parks. New York City has passed legislation recently prohibiting
smoking at all of the areas this bill encompasses.  Smoking is also
prohibited at children's playgrounds in the towns of Greenburgh (West-
chester), Huntington (Suffolk) and the City of Little Falls (Herkimer).
Many localities throughout the nation, including San Francisco, Los
Angles, and Salt Lake City have already acted to restrict or prohibit
smoking in parks.

Support for restricting smoking in outdoor areas has grown due to the
concerns of secondhand smoke and cigarette litter. Secondhand smoke
kills approximately 63,000 people each year. A survey conducted as part
of the 2005 Independent Evaluation of the Tobacco Control Program found
that a majority of New Yorkers support banning smoking at public parks.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2018: S5210 Committed to Rules

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

Fines created by this bill would result in some revenue for munici-
palities and localities that enforce the fine.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect 90 days after it shall have become a law.

AN ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to prohibiting smoking in
certain outdoor areas
B.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S2655B

SPONSOR: STAVISKY
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the public health law, in relation to
prohibiting smoking in certain outdoor areas

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This bill would restrict smoking in certain outdoor areas.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

  Section 1 amends the public health law 1399-O-2 by prohibiting smoking
on  any  municipal  or  state operated park. Municipal or state operated
park  include  beaches,  boardwalks,  marinas,  playgrounds,  recreation
centers,  group  camps  and all other property, equipment, buildings and
facilities that are located at  or  on  any  property  under  charge  or
control of any state or local government.

  Section 1 of this bill also labels areas where the provision shall not
apply.  These  areas  are sidewalks immediately adjoining parks, parking
lots, theatrical productions, any route through any park  strip,  median
or  mall  that  is  adjacent to vehicular traffic, any portion of a park
that is not used for park purposes, except when smoking has been specif-
ically prohibited in a state park or portion thereof by  the  office  of
parks,  recreation and historic preservation.  This section also exempts
the Adirondack park and Catskill park as defined by  section  9-0101  of
the environmental conservation law from any provisions of this bill. The
section also allows for applicability of any other laws to such places.

  Section 2 amends section 1399-v of the public health law. It assigns a
civil penalty of fifty dollars for each violation.

  Section 3 of this bill sets the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Worldwide  smokers  toss  an  estimated  4.5  trillion butts every year.
Cigarette butts have been the leading item  found  during  the  Interna-
tional  Coastal  Cleanup  Project.  (Conducted  by the Center for Marine
Conservation) Cigarette butts are not biodegradable. While the paper and
tobacco of cigarette butts. are biodegradable, their  cellulose  acetate
filters  are  not.  Cellulose acetate, a form of plastic, can persist in
the environment for many years.

Support for restricting smoking in outdoor areas has grown  due  to  the
concerns  of  secondhand  smoke  and  cigarette litter. Secondhand smoke
kills approximately 63,000 people each year. A survey conducted as  part
of  the 2005 Independent Evaluation of the Tobacco Control Program found
that a majority of New Yorkers support banning smoking at public parks.

Localities throughout the state of New York are now acting to ban  smok-
ing  in  public  parks. New York City has passed legislation prohibiting
smoking at all of the areas this bill encompasses. New York State  Parks
have  prohibited smoking in areas outline in this bill and beyond. Smok-
ing is prohibited in certain localities in 57 counties in the State  and
almost  every  county  has  some locality with some public playground or
park policies. This bill would  implement  a  statewide  prohibition  on

smoking in public parks keeping such precious places clean and safe from
smoking.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2017-18 - A.837 - Referred to Codes/S.5210 - Referred to Rules
2015-16 - A.1148 - Referred to Health/S.3171 - Referred to Health
2013-14 - A.450-B - Referred to Health/S.464-B - Referred to Health
2011-12 - A.6156A - Reported to Codes/S.6564 - Referred to Health

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

Fines  created  by  this  bill  would result in some revenue for munici-
palities and localities that enforce the fine.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the ninetieth  day  after  it  shall  have
become a law.

summary: Prohibits smoking in public parks; sets $50 fine; defines terms.
